headline: Defend the Indefensible — Persuasive Speaking Game for ESL Classes
outcomes: Students practise spontaneous persuasive speaking — forming and delivering arguments under time pressure with no preparation
Build resilience and fluency: students must speak even when they disagree with their assigned position, a real-world skill for debate and negotiation
Develop listening and critical evaluation as classmates react live to each argument with audience votes
Exposure to the language of concession, contrast, and hedging — 'admittedly', 'despite this', 'you could argue' — in a high-stakes context
howItWorks: The AI generates a wild or controversial statement — students are randomly assigned to DEFEND or ATTACK it
Each speaker has one minute to make their case while classmates watch on the teacher screen
Audience members react live on their devices — votes accumulate in real time as the speech unfolds
The student with the most audience reactions wins the round; the teacher can add commentary before revealing the next statement
teacherUseCases: Speaking fluency sprint — forces students to produce extended, connected speech without a script or preparation time
Debate preparation — run Defend the Indefensible as a warm-up before a formal debate unit to lower inhibition around arguing positions you don't personally hold
Opinion language practice — the game creates natural demand for concession phrases, modal verbs of possibility, and hedging expressions

faq.q: What if a student is assigned a position they find offensive?
faq.a: Statements are intentionally absurd and playful rather than genuinely controversial — designed to provoke laughter and creative thinking, not real debate. The teacher can skip any statement using the Skip button before it's shown to the class.

faq.q: Do shy students have to speak?
faq.a: The teacher controls assignment and can manually swap students between DEFEND and ATTACK — or volunteer a speaker rather than using random assignment. Students who aren't speaking are always engaged as the live audience.

faq.q: How does the audience voting work?
faq.a: While a student speaks, their classmates tap reaction buttons on their devices. Reactions accumulate live on the teacher screen — the speaker can see the count climbing (or stalling) in real time. Final vote totals determine the round winner.

faq.q: Can I use custom statements instead of AI-generated ones?
faq.a: Yes — teachers can type their own statements into the statement field before each round. This is useful if you want to tie the debate positions directly to the lesson topic or a specific text the class has been reading.

faq.q: How many rounds fit in a lesson?
faq.a: A 10-minute session covers 3 rounds comfortably. With 5 rounds and longer speeches, plan for 20 minutes. Each round generates a new statement automatically so there's no preparation between rounds.
